steps.action:
# The Last Light

Edmund had kept the light for thirty-one years, and in all that time, the sea had never once asked his opinion.

He climbed the iron stairs each evening at dusk — one hundred and twelve steps, which he counted not from habit but from devotion, the way a monk fingers a rosary. At the top, he would trim the wick, check the glass, and set the great lens turning with the patience of someone who understood that patience was its own kind of strength.

People in the village thought he must be lonely. They sent their children up the rocky path with casseroles and good intentions. Edmund accepted both graciously and ate alone, watching the beam sweep across the black water like a slow, generous hand.

He had been married once. Clara had lasted two winters before the isolation carved something out of her that she couldn't replace. He didn't blame her. The lighthouse asked everything and returned only purpose — a transaction not everyone could afford.

One November, a freighter lost its bearing in a sudden squall. Edmund saw her running wrong, tilting toward the hidden rocks his charts called Widow's Teeth. He increased the signal, flashing the sequence for danger until his hands shook.

The freighter corrected. Slowly, then decisively, she swung north toward open water and safety.

Edmund never learned the names of the people aboard. He never learned if anyone had even noticed the warning or simply stumbled right by accident. It didn't matter.

He descended the stairs — one hundred and twelve steps — made himself tea, and listened to the storm rage beautifully against the glass.

The light kept turning.

That was enough.
